idiom_name: `data class` + compiler-generated `copy()` (shallow); hand-written `clone()`/deep-copy for open hierarchies
implementation_notes: For the statically typed case Kotlin removes the pattern: `data class` generates `copy()` with default arguments, so 'clone and change a field' is `val older = jack.copy(age = 2)` with named arguments. The copy is shallow by contract (the docs show a shared `MutableList` changed through both objects), so reference members must be copied explicitly. Copying through a base type still needs hand-written code, because `copy()` is generated per data class and is not polymorphic; `java.lang.Cloneable`/`clone()` is inherited JVM machinery - protected in `Object`, requiring a public override that returns `Any` and must be cast, and it silently gives the wrong type when a subclass forgets to override. Declaring an interface method `fun Clone(): Shape` (or a sealed hierarchy with an exhaustive `when`) is the Kotlin shape of the pattern.
pitfalls: `copy()` is shallow: a `MutableList`/array/nested object property is shared between original and copy, so mutating one is visible through the other (the behaviour the data-class documentation calls out explicitly).

`copy()` exists only on data classes and cannot be declared or overridden by hand (the compiler rejects an explicit `copy()`); a polymorphic or deep variant therefore needs its own name, and an interface-typed reference cannot call `copy()` at all.

`Cloneable`/`Object.clone()` is protected in the JVM class, must be made public by an explicit override, returns `Any` that callers must cast, and any subclass that forgets to override silently returns the wrong runtime type.
